title: Ya-Sin, whole
hook: the messengers, the man who ran, the signs, the return (Surah 36)
tomorrow: what question does one surah ask again and again?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Hujurat: nations and tribes made so that you'd know one another. Today a man runs across a whole city to reach his own people.
screen: `KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` → `A MAN RUNS TO HIS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: When someone bursts into a room out of breath, every head turns. In Ya-Sin, a town has turned away the messengers sent to it and threatened them with stoning. Then, in Pickthall's words: "And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent!" He isn't one of the messengers. He's one of the townspeople. Why run? The answer hides in a strange gap a few lines later.
screen: `EVERY HEAD TURNS.` → `A MAN, RUNNING.` → `A STRANGE GAP.`

segments.voice: He speaks his piece: why shouldn't I serve the One who made me, and to whom you'll all return? Then the surah cuts. No scene of what his people did to him. The next line is simply: it was said, enter the Garden. Commentators fill the silence; the text leaves it. And his very first words there? Would that my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me. Not revenge. Not relief. He still wants good for the people who turned on him. That's the puzzle's answer: he ran because they were his. From there Ya-Sin turns to signs. Dead earth brought to life. Night stripped from day. "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit." Then the return. A man picks up an old, crumbled bone and asks who could revive bones like this. The answer: the One who made them the first time. And the line: "But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is." Here's something to tell a friend, with its honest label: a report in Tirmidhi calls Ya-Sin the heart of the Qur'an, and scholars grade that report weak. What the surah itself shows is enough: a man who cared about his people past the end, and a word that begins things again.
screen: `THE SURAH LEAVES A SILENCE.` · `WOULD THAT MY PEOPLE KNEW.` · `SUN, MOON, EACH IN AN ORBIT.` · `WHO REVIVES OLD BONES?` · then, large: `BE, AND IT IS.`

segments.voice: For the sit, listen to one sound: a recitation if you have one ready, or your own breathing if you don't. If there's someone you've lost, let them be near while you listen. Some Muslims read Ya-Sin for those who have died; anyone can simply remember.
screen: `LISTEN TO ONE SOUND.` · `LET SOMEONE BE NEAR.`

segments.voice: Ya-Sin. Two Arabic letters that open surah 36: the messengers, the man who ran, the signs, and the return.
Hold onto this: be, and it is, the word that made things first and can make them again. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ya-Sin for the dying and for those who have died, and at gatherings after a death, following reports that scholars grade differently; others read it at any time.

fork.setup: your little cousin asks why the man in Ya-Sin ran across the city. the best answer from the surah?

chat.says: read ya-sin w dadi for auntie nasreen. dadi keeps saying 'be, and it is.' how is that comforting??
options: Ya-Sin asks who revives old bones and answers: the One who made them first. That's her calm.
It means everything happens instantly, so grief should pass quickly too if you trust enough.
It's only about creation at the very start, so it doesn't really say anything about death.
chat.meaning: In Ya-Sin, 'Be! and it is' answers the question of who revives crumbled bones: the One who made them the first time.

sources.ref: Qur'an 36:13–27 (the town, the messengers, the man who ran, 'enter the Garden'), 36:33–37 (dead earth, night and day), 36:77–79 (the crumbled bone)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2887 (Ya-Sin as the heart of the Qur'an; graded weak)

notes: Pickthall 36:20, 36:40 and 36:82 match earlier days (549, 550, 551); confirm.

Paraphrased: the threat of stoning (36:18), 'why should I not serve Him who created me, and unto whom ye will be brought back' (36:22), 'It was said: Enter paradise' and 'Would that my people knew...' (36:26–27), dead earth revived (36:33), night stripped from day (36:37), the man with the crumbled bone and 'He will revive them Who produced them at the first' (36:78–79). Confirm.
Gentle line for parents: the man's death is not described; the voice says 'the surah cuts' and 'commentators fill the silence; the text leaves it'. Confirm handling.

Tirmidhi 2887 ('everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin') is graded weak by many hadith scholars; the voice labels it as such. Confirm number and grading wording. howItsDone's reports on reciting Ya-Sin for the dying (e.g. Abu Dawud 3121) are also graded differently.
